extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters/beat reporters covering city hall (municipal reporters)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for reporters who cover municipal government (city hall) about whom to contact, how to gather records and tips, how to interpret meetings and forecasts, and how to avoid common reporting pitfalls on the city beat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive (policy-making) — know sources of mayoral power
rubrics_metrics.description: The mayor derives authority from two powers: vetoing council work and appointing departmental executives. How much real power the mayor wields hinges on (a) his personal relations with the city council and (b) specifications of the city charter (veto-override vote size and appointment powers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should assess both personal/political dynamics with the council and the charter's formal powers when judging the mayor's influence. Note that sometimes the mayor is taciturn and policy explanations come from associates.

rubrics_metrics.name: City manager vs mayor — identify de facto policy originators
rubrics_metrics.description: A city manager, nominally executing council orders, through personal prowess and knowledge may originate policy; yet officially the manager's authority often ends with the right to recommend while the council retains enforcement power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn whether a city has both mayor and manager and which one is the ritualistic figure vs the working executive to know who to approach for policy and operational information.

rubrics_metrics.name: City council as ultimate authority — legislative structure and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The council is the sole custodian of authority to make municipal laws; smaller cities may have unicameral councils while larger ones may have two divisions. Proposed legislation is referred to standing or special committees which report to the full membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the council's structure (unicameral/bicameral), committee processes, and tactics (e.g., killing proposals by keeping them in committee or repeatedly referring them for further study). This informs how to follow, forecast, and interpret proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the liaison officers — city clerk's central information role
rubrics_metrics.description: The city clerk is clerk/secretary to the council; it is his duty to know the status of proposed legislation and to list items on the 'call' or 'order' for council meetings. He is often best able to predict the fate of a proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate the clerk as a primary source for meeting agendas, item status, and identification of speakers; use the clerk to get the 'call' and follow rapid meeting items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the city messenger & other low-level sources as clearing houses
rubrics_metrics.description: The city messenger, though seemingly minor, is in close touch with departments and can rival the clerk as an information source; reporters often start the day with a chat with the messenger who tells 'what's in the air.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate and cultivate a one-man clearing house (messenger or longtime employee) early on; they provide tips, directions to the right people, and early leads—though they may not supply complete attribution-ready quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand record-keeping and license officers — where the records live
rubrics_metrics.description: Record-keeping and license-granting are diffused across departments; which officer keeps which records and issues which permits varies by city and must be learned anew.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which departments hold birth/death/marriage lists, building permits, health reports, etc. Regularly visit record offices (daily or as appropriate) to gather routine, reliable stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish municipal-service vs technical/engineering matters (categories V and VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some municipal questions are public-service/administrative and others are technical/engineering. For category V ask control-board members; for category VI go to working personnel first and consult control-board members if overlap seems likely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose sources appropriate to the category: ask policy/control-level contacts for service decisions, and technical staff for engineering/implementation questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know enforcement systems: licensing, inspection, and protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Municipal observance is obtained by licensing (permits), inspection (e.g., sealer of weights and measures), and protection (police and fire). The character and strictness of licensing/inspection vary by city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should learn which departments handle licensing and inspections, how they operate, and the degree of enforcement in their city to judge stories (e.g., milk quality, building wiring inspections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand legal roles — city attorney vs clerk's informal guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The city attorney acts as trial lawyer and municipal attorney-general, ruling on ordinance interpretations and legal ramifications. The city clerk, through long tenure and contact, can provide informal but substantial legal analysis (quoted indirectly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know whom to ask for formal legal rulings (city attorney) and when to use anonymous paraphrase/roundabout references from the clerk ('sources close to city hall believed') if the attorney can't or won't speak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn municipal financial language and officials' roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessors determine tax rates, collectors receive tax money, treasurers/comptrollers handle books and bonds, and auditors verify books. Municipal nomenclature (boards, commissions, departments) can be confusing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid misinterpretation of financial announcements by learning the local financial terminology and context (e.g., boundary changes affecting tax totals). Cultivate trust with financial officials who may be cautious about talking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat public welfare arrangements as locally specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Public welfare departments can span record-keeping, municipal service, enforcement, legal, and financial functions; relief systems differ so greatly between communities they cannot be safely summarized generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters must learn how their particular city handles welfare and not assume uniformity across cities; check which divisions handle which aspects locally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate and personalize sources — learn people's peculiarities
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn personal peculiarities of officials (who likes to be kidded, who is formal, who will talk baseball and then provide stories) and handle each individually rather than with a standardized approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt interaction style to each official to build rapport; some are daily contacts while others need less frequent visits. Use favors/pleasantries appropriately (e.g., cigarettes with an assessor) but ethically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularly visit record offices and classify offices by news production
rubrics_metrics.description: Daily visits to offices where records are kept (marriage lists, permits, contagious disease cases) provide routine stories. Gradually classify offices by how often they produce news and schedule visits accordingly, ensuring notification if news breaks between visits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a schedule (daily, several times daily, weekly, fortnightly) based on an office's news output; before reducing visit frequency, ensure a mechanism exists for timely alerts of breaking news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask specific, seasonally informed questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Random 'What's going on today?' queries yield 'Nothing.' Knowing department seasonal cycles (e.g., early February is time to ask about street improvement lists) lets a reporter ask specific questions that reveal news or impending actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study normal departmental activities and calendars to spot unusual developments early; specificity is essential to avoid being newsless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle underlings' tips carefully and seek official confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Underlings may give tips but are not policy-makers and may warn against being quoted. Use their information as leads but go to superintendents or authorized officials for official statements. If an official refuses to speak, use tips judiciously without hinting sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a supervisor says 'Nothing to say,' the reporter may still use the story if properly sourced/phrased but must avoid revealing the original source; weigh expediency against risking future access or retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overpoliticizing routine municipal actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not interpret all council actions solely through party labels; many votes cross party lines (e.g., North-Side vs South-Side) and suggesting perpetual party control can harm institutions by misrepresenting motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve partisan explanations for occasions when politics clearly dominate; be cautious about imputing party motive to permanent/semipermanent municipal employees without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forecast stories appropriately — choose factual, interpretive, or predictive formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Forecasts fall into: factual forecast (safe, lists agenda items), interpretive forecast (assesses possible significance; requires good sizing-up), and ultimate predictive forecast (predicts votes/outcomes; for experts only). Background interpretation (history + guarded forecasting) is a safer step beyond factual forecasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use factual forecasts when novice; move to interpretive forecasts only with solid knowledge; reserve definitive predictions of votes/outcomes for highly experienced reporters and use background interpretation with careful qualifications to avoid embarrassing errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't over-rely on 'easy-to-quote' officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoting the same three or four vocal aldermen repeatedly can misrepresent council sentiment and elevate minority voices as 'men who count.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample broadly; seek a range of voices so reporting reflects the council's true balance. Avoid letting convenience bias shape perceived importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensationalizing advance stories to impress editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing an overstated advance to get editors to give later coverage page i status can lead to false expectations (e.g., inventing 'opening gun' campaigns from tentative remarks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be accurate and restrained in advance pieces. Exaggeration to please editors may damage credibility when the later story shows the event was dull.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for rapid, terse council meeting procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Council meetings often move quickly with mumbled routine items and rapid voice votes; 'passed by voice vote' is common, larger proposals may use hand raises or standing counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain the clerk's 'call' in advance, sit near the press table/clerk, use whispered questions or pencil notes during meetings, and follow up with the clerk after rapid items to ensure accuracy of votes and identifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn to identify council members and speakers quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize aldermen by faces rather than fixed seating; use the clerk or presiding officer to identify private citizens testifying; consider a pact with the presiding officer to have speakers identify themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice identification to reduce stage fright and ensure correct attribution in reports; ask the clerk for help when unsure.
